PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 94 — Lesson 118: Insomnia, Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Sleep Safety

FNP-level goal: Identify why a patient is not sleeping or is not alert, distinguish insomnia from sleep-disordered breathing and other disorders, prioritize safety risks such as drowsy driving or sedative harm, and build a treatment plan that is behavioral, medical, and longitudinal rather than a reflex medication refill.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate insomnia disorder, insufficient sleep opportunity, circadian misalignment, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), restless legs symptoms, parasomnias, and medication or substance-related sleep problems.
  • Conduct a focused sleep history that captures sleep timing, wake time, sleep opportunity, snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime function, mood, pain, substances, work schedule, medications, and safety risk.
  • Recognize OSA risk and use screening tools appropriately without treating a score or consumer device result as a diagnosis.
  • Explain why CBT-I is a primary treatment for chronic insomnia and why sleep-hygiene advice alone is usually inadequate.
  • Select the appropriate testing or referral pathway for suspected OSA, complex insomnia, parasomnia, narcolepsy symptoms, and dangerous daytime sleepiness.

Part 1 — Start With the Sleep Complaint, Not the Sleep Medication

“I cannot sleep” may mean difficulty falling asleep, difficulty staying asleep, early awakening, sleeping at the wrong biological time, sleeping too little because of work or caregiving, or sleeping many hours without feeling restored. “I am tired” may mean sleepiness, fatigue, depression, anemia, pain, medication effect, endocrine disease, cardiopulmonary disease, or burnout. The first FNP task is to define the symptom and its impact on driving, work, school, caregiving, falls, mood, and relationships.

Ask for the usual bedtime, estimated sleep onset, awakenings, wake time, naps, days off versus workdays, and what the patient does when awake. Ask whether there is enough time and a safe environment for sleep. A patient working rotating shifts may have circadian misalignment rather than primary insomnia. A patient who sleeps only five hours because of competing demands needs a different plan from one who spends nine hours in bed unable to sleep.

Part 2 — A Focused Sleep History

Ask about loud habitual snoring, witnessed pauses, gasping or choking, morning headache, dry mouth, nocturia, reflux, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness, drowsy driving, resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, weight change, and family history. Ask about restless uncomfortable leg sensations that are worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement; these may point toward restless legs syndrome. Ask about nightmares, sleepwalking, dream enactment, injury, sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep, and sudden emotion-triggered weakness.

Review caffeine, alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, stimulants, sedatives, opioids, antihistamines, antidepressants, blood-pressure medications, and over-the-counter sleep products. Medication and substance effects can be a cause, a partial treatment, or a source of harm. Also screen for depression, anxiety, trauma, bipolar-spectrum symptoms, suicidality, chronic pain, reflux, urinary symptoms, asthma/COPD symptoms, and menopausal symptoms when clinically relevant.

Part 3 — Chronic Insomnia Is Not a Failure of Willpower

Insomnia disorder includes difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or waking too early, despite adequate opportunity for sleep, with clinically meaningful daytime impairment. It often coexists with medical and psychiatric illness, but coexisting conditions do not make the sleep complaint less real. A patient can have insomnia and OSA at the same time; do not assume one diagnosis eliminates the other.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured treatment that targets perpetuating thoughts and behaviors, stimulus control, sleep scheduling, relaxation, and other evidence-based components. It is more than generic sleep hygiene. Sleep-hygiene advice can support care, but telling a patient to avoid screens and drink tea is usually not a complete treatment for chronic insomnia. Discuss access barriers and consider qualified in-person, telehealth, or validated digital options as locally available.

Part 4 — Medication Safety in Insomnia

Medication may have a role for selected patients, but the choice should follow diagnosis and an explicit discussion of duration, benefit, harm, interactions, driving, alcohol and opioid use, pregnancy considerations, fall risk, cognitive risk, respiratory risk, and follow-up. Sedating products can worsen next-day impairment, falls, confusion, and respiratory suppression—especially in older adults or people with untreated sleep-disordered breathing, chronic lung disease, opioid exposure, or multiple sedating medicines.

Do not prescribe a sedative merely because the schedule is full. Avoid abrupt changes to medicines with dependence or withdrawal potential without a patient-specific plan. The goal is to reduce disability safely, not to create a second problem of daytime sedation, tolerance, or interaction-related harm.

Part 5 — Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Common, Treatable, and Not Diagnosed by Snoring Alone

OSA involves recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep. Symptoms may include loud snoring, witnessed apnea, choking or gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Some patients—particularly women, older adults, and people with comorbid insomnia—may present with fatigue, insomnia, mood symptoms, or hypertension rather than a classic snoring story.

Screening questionnaires can help identify risk and guide conversation, but they do not diagnose OSA. Body size alone does not diagnose or exclude OSA. A comprehensive sleep evaluation and appropriate diagnostic testing are required. Explain that a home device or wearable result can be useful information to bring to care but should not be treated as a final medical diagnosis without clinical interpretation.

Part 6 — HSAT Versus Polysomnography

Home sleep apnea testing (HSAT) may be appropriate for an uncomplicated adult with symptoms suggesting increased risk of moderate-to-severe OSA. It must be ordered as part of a medical evaluation, interpreted appropriately, and linked to follow-up. It is not a general screening test for asymptomatic populations and should not be interpreted from automatically generated data alone.

In-laboratory polysomnography is generally preferred when the patient has significant cardiopulmonary disease, possible sleep-related hypoventilation, neuromuscular weakness, chronic opioid use, a history of stroke, severe insomnia, or other complexity that can make HSAT insufficient. A negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate HSAT does not end the evaluation when clinical suspicion remains; further sleep testing may be needed.

Part 7 — Daytime Sleepiness Is a Safety Problem

Ask directly: Have you nodded off while driving, at a red light, at work, while holding a child, or during a safety-sensitive task? Excessive sleepiness can lead to motor-vehicle and occupational injury. Counsel the patient not to drive or operate dangerous equipment when sleepy and arrange timely assessment. This is practical harm reduction, not judgment.

When daytime sleepiness is severe, sudden, or associated with cataplexy-like episodes, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, or uncontrolled OSA symptoms, prompt sleep-medicine evaluation is appropriate. The FNP should also evaluate acute contributors such as medication effects, infection, metabolic derangement, hypoxia, and depression when clinically indicated.

Part 8 — Parasomnias and Sleep Movement Disorders

Dream enactment with injury risk, recurrent sleepwalking, violent behaviors in sleep, or possible nocturnal seizures requires a safety plan and specialty evaluation. Ask about injuries to the patient or bed partner, weapons or dangerous objects near the bed, substance use, medication changes, and neurologic symptoms. A safe sleep environment is an immediate intervention while diagnosis proceeds.

Restless legs symptoms may disrupt sleep onset and should prompt review of iron status and contributing medications or conditions when clinically appropriate. Do not confuse a generalized leg cramp, neuropathic pain, edema, or akathisia with classic restless legs without a detailed history.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Insomnia or Insufficient Sleep?

A 35-year-old says she has insomnia but works a rotating schedule, cares for children late at night, and sleeps seven hours only on weekends. The FNP recognizes inadequate and irregular sleep opportunity as a major driver, screens for mood and OSA symptoms, collaborates on schedule-protecting changes, and avoids labeling her with chronic insomnia before the sleep opportunity problem is addressed.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Snoring Patient With Safety Risk

A 52-year-old with hypertension has loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches, and has nearly fallen asleep while driving home. Screening supports high risk, but it is not the diagnosis. The FNP discusses immediate driving safety, arranges appropriate diagnostic evaluation, reviews sedating medications and alcohol, and documents a clear plan for follow-up and treatment initiation.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Negative Home Test

A patient with severe insomnia, chronic opioid therapy, and persistent choking awakenings has a negative home sleep test. The test does not close the case. The patient is not an uncomplicated HSAT candidate, and the persistent clinical concern requires sleep-specialty guidance and a more appropriate diagnostic pathway.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Define the problem: insomnia, inadequate opportunity, circadian issue, sleepiness, breathing disorder, movement disorder, parasomnia, or medication effect.
  2. Measure impact: daytime function, driving, occupation, falls, mood, cardiovascular risk, and bed-partner safety.
  3. Look for OSA: snoring, witnessed apnea, gasping, sleepiness, hypertension, arrhythmia, and risk context—but do not diagnose from a screen alone.
  4. Treat chronic insomnia appropriately: CBT-I is foundational; sleep hygiene alone is not a full intervention; medication requires risk-benefit review and follow-up.
  5. Match testing to complexity: HSAT for selected uncomplicated high-risk adults; polysomnography or sleep-medicine referral when complexity or an inconclusive test demands it.
  6. Escalate safety threats: drowsy driving, serious parasomnia injury, hypoxia, severe sleepiness, and symptoms suggesting narcolepsy or another serious disorder need prompt action.

Take-Home Summary

Good sleep care begins with a precise sleep history, not a sedative prescription. Insomnia, OSA, circadian disruption, restless legs, parasomnias, pain, mood, and medications frequently overlap. The FNP improves outcomes by identifying daytime safety risk, using CBT-I as a primary chronic-insomnia treatment, selecting sleep testing appropriately, avoiding harmful medication combinations, and ensuring that diagnostic results lead to actual follow-through.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, current prescribing information, sleep-study interpretation, behavioral sleep-medicine care, specialty consultation, or emergency evaluation when immediate safety risks are present.
